tagline: Limestone towns and farmland connect Grant Wood country to the Mississippi.
intro: The paved Grant Wood Scenic Byway runs 80 miles from Stone City to the Mississippi River through farmland, limestone bluffs and wetlands. Iowa’s byways guide includes it among the state byways. Travel Iowa emphasizes the connection between this countryside and Grant Wood, linking his hometown with places that inspired his work. The route connects the Wapsipinicon, Maquoketa and Mississippi rivers. The Iowa guide identifies a ridge on Iowa 64 and Bellevue State Park’s overlook among the places to take in the landscape.

At its western end, Stone City began as a company town for quarry workers. As railroads expanded, its limestone reached neighboring states for bridges, bridge piers and building foundations. Portland cement production in Waterloo in 1905 brought competition, and the quarries began closing. The quarry owner’s estate took on another role in 1932, when Wood, Edward Rowan and Adrian Dornbush established an art colony there. Quarrying revived under a new owner in 1952, and Stone City again shipped its limestone across the country.

Start at Stone City’s limestone buildings, then continue to Anamosa and its castle-like working penitentiary. Farther east, the byway includes Wyoming and Maquoketa before reaching Bellevue on the Mississippi. There, North and South Bluffs frame the town’s valley, and Lock and Dam No. 12 lies along its riverfront.

moments.title: Stone City
moments.text: An art colony made new use of quarry owner John Green’s estate in 1932. Grant Wood, Edward Rowan and Adrian Dornbush leased ten acres with little more than $100 and promissory notes. The mansion’s upper floor became a dormitory, while Dornbush lived in an apartment in the water tower. The colony never succeeded financially. The mansion was damaged by fire in 1963 and demolished in the 1990s. The water tower and ice house survived, converted into private homes. The leased property also supplied business offices, a kitchen and a sculpture studio in the mansion.

moments.title: Anamosa State Penitentiary
moments.text: Anamosa’s prison walls were built with forced labor. After Iowa commissioned the additional penitentiary in 1872, officials bought an eleven-acre site and a quarry for building stone. Twenty prisoners arrived from Fort Madison in spring 1873 to work on construction. Architects William Foster and Henry Franz Liebbe designed its Scottish Baronial Revival walls and crenelated towers. The prison began operating in 1874 and still houses inmates. Stone lions mark the central Administration Building’s entrance. Outside the walls, the prison museum occupies a stone building previously used as a barn and cheese-making facility.
moments.notice: Crenelated towers rise above the outer walls; stone lions mark the Administration Building’s entrance.

moments.title: Bellevue
moments.text: Bellevue fits between North and South Bluffs, with the Mississippi along its eastern edge and the Mill Creek valley extending west. River steamboats once stopped at a grand staircase connecting the riverbank with the higher Riverfront Park, transferring passengers and goods. Riverboat travel diminished toward the middle of the twentieth century. The town remains beside Lock and Dam No. 12. Bellevue State Park and its overlook are among the byway’s documented scenic viewpoints. U.S. 52 follows Riverview Drive through town, meeting Iowa 62 at State Street. Freight trains also run along a railway dividing Second Street.
